title: THE FOUR LAYERS
subtitle: Silicon, Capital and the Companies That Own Artificial Intelligence — How Chips, Clouds, Models and Apps Became the World's Most Valuable Industry
author: Tang Shiuan Jenn

content_policy.sourcing: EVERY figure — market capitalisation, revenue, valuation, headcount, market share, share-price move, investment amount — must be given WITH the date it refers to AND a named source in the text (e.g. 'as at August 2026, per company filings' or 'reported by CNBC in November 2025'). A figure without a date and a source may not appear.
content_policy.no_invention: Never invent or estimate a figure. If a number is not verifiable, say plainly that it is not disclosed. Do not interpolate, do not round from memory, do not present an estimate as a fact.
content_policy.illustrative_examples: Worked examples using round invented numbers ARE allowed to teach a mechanism, but must be labelled explicitly as illustrative and not attributed to any company.
content_policy.no_advice: This book is not investment advice and says so. It never recommends buying or selling any security, never gives a price target, and never predicts a share price. It teaches the reader to read the numbers themselves.
content_policy.no_allegation: Where a structure invites suspicion (circular revenue, vendor financing, investing in customers), explain the mechanism and what to watch for. Never allege improper conduct by a named company beyond what public disclosure supports.
content_policy.staleness: The book states openly and repeatedly that its figures are snapshots that will be out of date, and shows the reader where to find the current number.
content_policy.geopolitics: Describe export controls, Taiwan and state capital factually. No advocacy, no speculation about conflict, no political sides.
content_policy.author_anecdotes: No first-person anecdotes claiming specific professional experience. Chapter openings are second-person or generic professional scenes.

parts.title: How to Read This Industry
parts.summary: The tools. Four layers, what the numbers mean, and why every figure in this book carries a date.

chapters.title: The Four Layers

art.title: The AI stack, bottom to top
labels: Model layer — where intelligence is made
Semiconductor layer — where it is physically possible

chapters.brief: Open the book on a single machine and follow the money down through it: a person types a question, an application takes the payment, a model answers, a data centre runs it, and somewhere a chip does the arithmetic. Establish the four-layer frame that organises the entire book and explain why the value has been moving DOWN the stack, not up. State the book's method plainly: every company is examined on origin, strategy, accounts, challenge, opportunity. State the honesty rule that governs the book: every figure carries a date and a source, because a market capitalisation is a photograph, not a fact.

chapters.title: What a Market Capitalisation Actually Is

art.title: Inside a market capitalisation
labels: What it is NOT: money the company has

chapters.brief: The most quoted number in this industry is the least understood. Explain market cap as price times shares, why it is a claim about the future rather than a measure of the present, why it moves without anything happening inside the company, and why comparing two companies' market caps tells you less than comparing their cash flows. Use the real August 2026 ranking as the worked example. Make the reader permanently sceptical of headlines that lead with market cap.

chapters.title: Reading a Chip Company's Accounts

art.title: What to look at first in a semiconductor company
labels: Gross margin and what drives it
R&D as a share of revenue

chapters.brief: The accountant's chapter. Walk through the line items that actually matter in a semiconductor business and what each one is trying to tell you: gross margin as the scoreboard of pricing power, capex as a bet placed years before revenue, inventory as the earliest warning of a turn, customer concentration as the risk nobody puts on the front page. Teach the reader to open a real filing and know where to look. No company-specific figures here — this is the toolkit.

chapters.title: Reading a Cloud Company's Accounts

art.title: How cloud capex becomes cloud profit
labels: Margin depends on the life assumed

chapters.brief: Cloud businesses are accounting businesses. Explain how a data centre becomes a balance-sheet asset, how the assumed useful life of a server changes reported profit without changing a single dollar of cash, why extending server life flattered earnings across the industry, and what to watch now that AI hardware may age faster than the assumptions. This chapter is the book's sharpest analytical tool and it belongs to the author's profession.

chapters.title: Reading a Company With No Accounts

art.title: Public company vs private lab
labels: Private: the last round sets the price

chapters.brief: Two of the most important companies in this book publish no audited accounts. Explain what a private valuation actually is — the price of the last shares sold, on terms you cannot see — why post-money valuation overstates worth when preferences and ratchets are attached, and how to read reported revenue run-rates that nobody has audited. Set the standard the book will apply to OpenAI and Anthropic: report what is disclosed, name who disclosed it, and never present it as equivalent to a filing.

chapters.title: Every Number in This Book Has a Date

art.title: Why a figure needs a timestamp

chapters.brief: A short, honest chapter that would not appear in most books on this subject. Explain the problem directly: this industry re-prices weekly, and a printed book cannot keep up. Set out the convention used throughout — figures are given with the date and the source, and the reader is shown where to look up the current number themselves. Argue that a book's job here is the durable part: structure, economics, incentives and history. The numbers are illustration, not foundation.

parts.title: The Semiconductor Layer
parts.summary: The bottom of the stack, where the physical limits live and where the whole industry's capacity is decided years in advance.

chapters.title: The Bottom of the Stack

art.title: Who does what in making a chip

chapters.brief: Establish the division of labour that most readers have never seen: the company that designs a chip usually does not make it, the company that makes it does not make the machines, and the company that makes the machines has no competitor. Explain fabless, foundry, IDM and OSAT plainly. Show why this structure creates chokepoints rather than a supply chain, and why a chokepoint is worth more than a market share.

chapters.title: TSMC: The Company Everything Runs Through
chapters.brief: The single most important company most people cannot name. History from 1987 and Morris Chang's insight that manufacturing could be a service rather than a by-product of design. Explain the pure-play foundry model, why it won, and how the leading edge became a natural monopoly. Give TSMC's position with dated figures — market capitalisation around 2.17 trillion US dollars as at August 2026, and 2026 capital expenditure guided to 52 to 56 billion dollars, above analyst expectations — and source both. Cover the challenge chapter: geographic concentration, Arizona and Japan expansion, cost of building outside Taiwan.

chapters.title: How a Foundry Actually Makes Money

art.title: Foundry economics
labels: Fab built with borrowed and retained cash
Yield climbs, cost per wafer falls
Price falls more slowly than cost

chapters.brief: The economics that decide the whole industry's capacity. Explain the wafer-price/yield curve, why a fab must run full, why the leading edge earns and the trailing edge grinds, and why capacity decisions taken today set the ceiling on AI three years out. Include a worked, clearly-labelled illustrative example with invented round numbers, stated plainly as illustrative and not as any company's figures.

chapters.title: ASML: One Machine, No Substitute

art.title: Why EUV has no second source
labels: No competing machine at the leading edge

chapters.brief: The most extreme chokepoint in modern industry. History from Philips spin-off to the EUV bet that took two decades and nearly failed. Explain why no competitor exists and why that is a technical fact rather than a commercial one. Dated figures: ASML crossed 500 billion US dollars in market value for the first time in January 2026; give the source. Cover export controls as an existential political exposure.

chapters.title: The Machines Behind the Machines
chapters.brief: The suppliers nobody outside the industry can name and every fab depends on. Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, Tokyo Electron. Explain what each step does in terms a non-engineer can follow, why this layer is a quiet oligopoly, why its revenue leads the foundries by roughly a year, and why watching equipment orders is the best early signal of the cycle turning.

chapters.title: Nvidia I: The Graphics Years, 1993 to 2006
chapters.brief: The origin story, told without hindsight. Three founders, a diner, and a company that nearly died on its first product. Correct the record on early backing: Nvidia's early investors were Sequoia Capital and Sutter Hill Ventures, not SoftBank. Cover the 1995 near-death, the RIVA 128 rescue, the GeForce launch and the naming of the GPU. End on CUDA in 2006 with the reader not yet knowing why it matters.

chapters.title: Nvidia II: The Decade Nobody Noticed

art.title: How CUDA became a moat
labels: A GPU is a parallel machine
CUDA lets ordinary programmers use it
Researchers adopt it because it is there

chapters.brief: The most valuable strategic decision of the period, made when it looked like an expensive distraction. Explain what CUDA is in plain terms, why a decade of unglamorous software investment created a switching cost that silicon alone never could, and how the 2012 deep-learning moment found the tooling already waiting. This is the chapter that explains the moat, and it is a software chapter in a hardware book.

chapters.title: Nvidia III: To the Largest Company on Earth
chapters.brief: The four years that re-rated the company. Cover the 2022 collapse honestly — the crypto bust and the inventory charge — because the book's credibility depends on including the bad years. Then the inflection. Dated: Nvidia was the world's most valuable company at roughly 5.3 to 5.4 trillion US dollars in August 2026; source it and state plainly that it will have moved by the time this is read.

chapters.title: Nvidia's Accounts, Line by Line

art.title: Reading Nvidia's filings as an accountant
labels: Gross margin and what it implies about pricing power

chapters.brief: Apply chapter three's toolkit to the most valuable company in the world. Walk the reader through what to look for in the filings, what the concentration disclosure means, why purchase commitments matter more than most readers realise, and why an investment in a customer deserves a second look. Teach the reading, do not simply report the numbers; and give the figures that are given with dates and a source.

chapters.title: AMD: The Long Second Place
chapters.brief: The best turnaround story in the industry and a lesson in what second place is worth. Cover the 2012 near-death, the balance-sheet repair, the decision to go all-in on a new architecture, and the strategic question of whether a credible second source can break a software moat. Dated market capitalisation with source.

chapters.title: Intel: How the Leader Lost the Lead

art.title: How a process lead is lost
labels: Integrated model wins for thirty years

chapters.brief: The cautionary tale the rest of the book needs. Explain the integrated device manufacturer model and why it was a genuine advantage, then how a process delay compounds into a structural loss. Treat Intel seriously and without mockery — this is a company that built the industry. Cover the foundry strategy and the government money honestly, and set out what would have to be true for it to work.

chapters.title: Broadcom: The Quiet Trillion
chapters.brief: The trillion-dollar company almost no consumer has heard of. Explain the roll-up strategy, the custom accelerator business that makes it the main alternative to buying merchant GPUs, and why the networking silicon matters as much as the accelerators once clusters get large. Dated market capitalisation with source. Cover the strategic question: is a customer that designs its own chip a customer or a future competitor?

chapters.title: Arm and SoftBank
chapters.brief: Correct the record and tell the better story. SoftBank's foundational chip bet was Arm in 2016, not an early stake in Nvidia. Explain the licensing model and why owning the instruction set is a different kind of asset. Then the Nvidia thread told accurately: the Vision Fund built a roughly 4.9 per cent stake in 2017 and sold it in January 2019 for about 3.3 billion dollars, a profit of roughly 2.6 billion; a later stake was sold in full in November 2025 for 5.83 billion to fund investment in OpenAI and Stargate. Source each. Draw the lesson about conviction, timing and what an exit costs.

chapters.title: Memory I: Why DRAM Was Always a Bad Business
chapters.brief: Before the supercycle, the history. Explain why memory was for decades the worst business in semiconductors: a commodity with brutal capital intensity, a cycle that destroyed more capital than it created, and a consolidation from dozens of makers to three that survived. This chapter exists so the reader understands exactly what changed.

chapters.title: Memory II: HBM and the Supercycle

art.title: Why AI broke the memory cycle
labels: HBM is hard to make and yields poorly
A commodity becomes a specified component

chapters.brief: The answer to the question the reader has been asking: why did memory share prices go up so much? Explain high-bandwidth memory in plain terms, why AI accelerators are limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw arithmetic, and why that turned a commodity into a qualified, contracted, sold-out component. Dated: the 2026 HBM market estimated at about 54.6 billion dollars, up roughly 58 per cent year on year; SK Hynix holding the largest share; HBM capacity reported sold out through 2026 across the major suppliers. Source each figure.

chapters.title: Three Companies, One Cycle

art.title: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron
labels: Samsung: scale, breadth, its own foundry
All three: capacity sold out, capex rising

chapters.brief: The three survivors examined side by side on strategy, position and exposure. Dated share-price moves for 2026 with their source, and the honest counterweight: memory is historically the most cyclical business in the industry, and a supercycle is still a cycle. Include SK Hynix's reported 38 billion dollar plant investment as the illustration of how the industry responds to a shortage — and what that response has always meant next.

parts.title: The Compute Layer
parts.summary: Where the chips are assembled into machines, financed, powered, and rented by the hour.

chapters.title: What Compute Means on a Balance Sheet
chapters.brief: Translate a building full of machines into an accountant's view. What is capitalised, over what life, and how each assumption flows to reported profit. Establish the number that will recur through the rest of the book: assumed useful life. Explain in plain terms how a small change to it moves billions of reported earnings without moving a cent of cash.

chapters.title: Microsoft Azure
chapters.brief: The company that turned an incumbent position into an AI position. History of the cloud pivot, why enterprise distribution is the hardest asset to replicate, and how the OpenAI relationship shaped the capex plan. Dated market capitalisation with source. Challenge chapter: capex intensity, the return question, and the strategic risk of depending on a partner that is also becoming a competitor.

chapters.title: Amazon Web Services

art.title: AWS from internal tool to profit engine

chapters.brief: The business that funded a retailer's entire strategy. Explain how AWS was built, why being first mattered less than being cheapest and most complete, and how the AI wave arrived with Amazon holding infrastructure but not a frontier model. Cover the Anthropic relationship and the custom-silicon strategy as two answers to the same problem.

chapters.title: Google Cloud and the TPU

art.title: Buying accelerators vs building them
labels: Merchant GPU: fast to adopt, priced by the seller
Custom silicon: years of investment, no seller's margin

chapters.brief: The only company that designed its own AI accelerator a decade before it needed one. Explain the Tensor Processing Unit, why Google built it, and what owning your own silicon does to your cost structure when demand explodes. Cover the strategic oddity of being simultaneously the most vertically integrated player and a large customer of the layer below.

chapters.title: Oracle's Second Act

art.title: An incumbent finds a new business

chapters.brief: How a company written off as a legacy vendor became a serious infrastructure player by taking a risk the larger clouds would not. Explain the strategy honestly, including the balance-sheet question: capacity built against contracted future revenue is a bet on the customer's survival as much as on demand.

chapters.title: The Neoclouds
chapters.brief: The companies that did not exist before this cycle. Explain the business model, the financing structures that make it possible, why lenders accept accelerators as collateral, and the risks that creates if the residual value of that collateral falls. Treat it analytically, not as either a scandal or a miracle.

chapters.title: Stargate and the Megaproject Era

art.title: How a multi-hundred-billion project is assembled
labels: A construction timeline nobody has attempted

chapters.brief: The scale that broke the old vocabulary. Explain what these joint ventures are structurally, who bears which risk, and why the capital comes from consortia rather than one balance sheet. Include SoftBank's stated funding of its participation partly from the November 2025 sale of its Nvidia stake, with source. Be clear about what is announced versus what is built.

chapters.title: Custom Silicon Everywhere
chapters.brief: Every large buyer is trying to become a maker. Explain why: not to beat the merchant supplier on performance but to escape its margin. Assess honestly what each programme has actually achieved versus announced, and what it takes to displace an incumbent whose real moat is software.

chapters.title: The Power Problem
chapters.brief: The constraint that is replacing chip supply as the binding one. Explain interconnection queues, why a signed power contract is now a strategic asset, why nuclear and gas re-entered the conversation, and how power availability is starting to decide where compute gets built. Avoid advocacy on energy policy; describe the engineering and the economics.

chapters.title: Depreciation: The Number That Decides Everything
chapters.brief: The book's central accounting chapter, and the one only an accountant would write. Explain how the industry extended assumed server lives, what that did to reported margins, and why AI hardware may not age the way general-purpose servers did. Set out precisely what the reader should watch in the disclosures and what a shortening of assumed life would do to reported profit across the sector. No prediction; a method.

parts.title: The Model Layer
parts.summary: Two private companies worth close to a trillion dollars each, and the giants trying to catch them.

chapters.title: What a Model Company Actually Sells

art.title: Where a model company's money comes from

chapters.brief: Before the histories, the business model. Explain the revenue lines, why gross margin depends on the cost of inference rather than the cost of training, why training is a capitalisable-looking cost that mostly is not capitalised, and why revenue growth and cash burn can both be enormous at once. Establish the reporting standard: these are private companies, and what is known is what they or their investors have chosen to say.

chapters.title: OpenAI I: 2015 to 2022
chapters.brief: The founding and the structure that would later cause so much difficulty. Explain the original mission, why the non-profit form could not raise what training required, and what the capped-profit structure was designed to do. End at the consumer launch that changed the industry's clock speed.

chapters.title: OpenAI II: The Microsoft Relationship

art.title: What each side supplied
labels: Both: a dependency neither fully controls

chapters.brief: The most consequential commercial relationship of the period, examined as a deal rather than a story. What each party contributed, what each received, how the exclusivity worked and how it loosened. Explain why a partnership between a supplier and a competitor is inherently unstable, and how both sides hedged.

chapters.title: OpenAI III: Restructuring and the Road to a Trillion
chapters.brief: The corporate and capital history brought current. Dated and sourced: OpenAI closed a 122 billion dollar round in March 2026 at an 852 billion dollar valuation, with Amazon reported as investing 50 billion in that round. Explain what a post-money valuation of that size does and does not tell you, why a rival cloud investing in it is strategically remarkable, and what an IPO would force into daylight.

chapters.title: Anthropic I: The Founding
chapters.brief: The founding, the reasons given for it, and the deliberate strategic differences: a safety-forward research posture and an enterprise-first commercial approach rather than a consumer land grab. Describe the positioning accurately and without taking a side on the underlying disagreement.

chapters.title: Anthropic II: Two Clouds, Two Investors
chapters.brief: The strangest ownership structure in the industry: two competing hyperscalers as major investors in the same company. Dated and sourced: Amazon with up to 33 billion dollars committed, Google with up to 43 billion including 10 billion in April 2026. Explain how such a structure is negotiated, what governance protections a company seeks, and why both investors accepted a minority position.

chapters.title: Anthropic III: Nearly a Trillion, and the IPO Question

art.title: Valuation history
labels: May 2026: 65 billion Series H at 965 billion post-money
Briefly the most valuable private company

chapters.brief: Bring it current with sources. Anthropic closed a 65 billion dollar Series H at a 965 billion dollar post-money valuation in May 2026, briefly surpassing OpenAI as the most valuable private company. Explain what such a round implies about expected revenue, what preferences attached to late rounds mean for the headline number, and what public reporting would change.

chapters.title: Google DeepMind and Gemini
chapters.brief: The company that owns every layer of the stack, and why that has been both an advantage and an obstacle. Cover the merger of research groups, the strategic cost of moving late in consumer AI while holding the strongest research position, and the question of whether integration or focus wins.

chapters.title: Meta, xAI and the Open-Weight Camp

art.title: Two strategies for the model layer
labels: Closed weights: sold access, protected margin
Open weights: given away, commoditises the rival

chapters.brief: Why a company would spend billions training a model and then give the weights away. Explain the strategic logic of commoditising your complement, Meta's position as a company that monetises attention rather than tokens, and xAI's different bet. Assess honestly what open weights have and have not achieved commercially.

chapters.title: The Chinese Labs
chapters.brief: The part of the industry most Western coverage handles badly. Describe the labs, the constraint that export controls place on the layer beneath them, and the research consequence: efficiency becomes the priority when capacity is capped. Report what is disclosed, avoid geopolitical advocacy, and be explicit about what is not verifiable from outside.

parts.title: The Application Layer
parts.summary: The top of the stack, where a user finally pays, and where the margin is fought over.

chapters.title: Where the Money Meets the User

art.title: Following one payment down the stack
labels: Chip vendor took its margin years earlier

chapters.brief: Trace a single monthly subscription all the way down the four layers and show who keeps what. This is the chapter that makes the book's structure concrete, and it sets up the margin argument that runs through this part.

chapters.title: Microsoft
chapters.brief: The company positioned at every layer of the stack. Financial position with dated figures and sources — roughly 3.66 trillion dollars market capitalisation in August 2026. Strategy, challenge and opportunity: distribution as the deepest moat, capex as the biggest question, and the tension of partnering with a company that competes with you.

chapters.title: Alphabet
chapters.brief: Dated market capitalisation with source — roughly 4.20 trillion dollars in August 2026. The strategic problem of defending a business that AI could disrupt while building the thing that disrupts it. Cover the integration advantage, the regulatory overhang, and the Anthropic stake as a hedge.

chapters.title: Amazon
chapters.brief: The company that owns the most infrastructure and the least frontier research, and how it bought its way to a position. Cover the Anthropic investment, the reported 50 billion dollar participation in OpenAI's 2026 round, and what it means to be a major investor in both leading labs. Source both.

chapters.title: Meta

art.title: Meta's different equation
labels: AI improves ad targeting and ranking

chapters.brief: The only giant whose AI spending is justified almost entirely by internal returns. Explain why that changes the analysis, why Meta can rationally give models away, and the risk of a capex programme whose payback is measured in engagement rather than invoices.

chapters.title: Apple: The Quiet One
chapters.brief: The most valuable company for years, and the least visible in this cycle. Dated market capitalisation with source — roughly 4.41 trillion dollars in August 2026. Explain the strategy of arriving late deliberately, the on-device argument, the silicon capability, and the genuine risk of being a distribution channel for someone else's intelligence.

chapters.title: The Incumbent Software Companies

art.title: How incumbents are responding
labels: Embed AI in the existing product
Reprice per seat or per outcome
Defend the data they already hold

chapters.brief: Salesforce, Adobe, SAP, ServiceNow and the rest. The strategic problem of being a software company when the software can increasingly be generated, and the defence that customer data and workflow, not features, are the moat.

chapters.title: The Application Startups

art.title: The thin-wrapper problem
labels: Grow fast on a good interface
Model provider ships the same feature

chapters.brief: Why so many application companies grew quickly and then struggled, and what distinguishes the ones that lasted. Explain the wrapper critique fairly, then the counter-argument: workflow, data and distribution are real assets even when the model is not yours.

chapters.title: What Users Actually Pay For

art.title: What a buyer is really buying
labels: A capability they could not buy before
A fear of being left behind

chapters.brief: An honest chapter about demand. Distinguish durable purchase reasons from cyclical ones, and be candid that some current spending is driven by competitive anxiety rather than measured return. This matters, because the whole capex programme below rests on this layer's revenue proving real.

chapters.title: The Margin Question

art.title: Where the profit ends up
labels: Chip vendor: high margin, taken first
Model layer: margin depends on inference cost
Application: margin depends on switching cost

chapters.brief: Close the part by asking the question the whole book circles: in the long run, which layer keeps the profit? Set out the arguments for each layer honestly, note that the answer has changed before in computing history, and refuse to predict. Give the reader the framework instead.

parts.title: The Web of Ownership
parts.summary: Who owns whom, what the cross-holdings mean, and how money moves in circles.

chapters.title: How to Read a Cross-Holding

art.title: Anatomy of a strategic stake
labels: What it obliges each side to do

chapters.brief: The toolkit for this part. Explain the difference between a passive investment, an equity method holding and control, why the accounting treatment changes the reported earnings of the investor, and why a stake accompanied by a supply agreement is a different animal from a stake alone.

chapters.title: Microsoft and OpenAI

art.title: The most examined relationship in technology

chapters.brief: The relationship examined clause by clause as far as public disclosure allows. What was invested, what was contributed in kind, what each side received, and how the arrangement changed. Be explicit about what is not public.

chapters.title: Amazon, Google and Anthropic
chapters.brief: How two competitors ended up funding the same company. Dated and sourced. Explain the commercial logic for each investor, what the compute commitments mean in practice, and the reported effect on the investors' own earnings — noting that stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI have been reported as distorting the corporate earnings picture for the companies holding them.

chapters.title: Nvidia as an Investor

art.title: A supplier with equity in its customers

chapters.brief: The chapter that requires the most care. Nvidia has taken equity positions across its own customer base. Set out what is disclosed, explain neutrally why a dominant supplier might invest in demand for its product, and explain what an analyst should watch for without alleging anything the filings do not support.

chapters.title: Circular Revenue

art.title: When money goes round
labels: Cash has moved in a circle

chapters.brief: The pattern that most worries careful readers of this industry. Explain the mechanism in accounting terms, why it is not automatically improper, what disclosure and revenue-recognition rules require, and what specifically to look for. Reference the historical precedent from the telecom equipment era. Make claims about mechanism, not about any named company's conduct.

chapters.title: Vendor Financing, Old and New

art.title: A pattern that has happened before

chapters.brief: The historical rhyme, examined properly. What vendor financing did to the telecom equipment industry, how today's structures differ, and where they are similar. Be even-handed: state the case that it is different, and the case that it is not.

chapters.title: SoftBank

art.title: One investor across the whole stack

chapters.brief: The single most instructive investor case study in the book, told accurately with every figure sourced. The Arm acquisition, the Nvidia stake bought in 2017 and sold in 2019 for about 3.3 billion at a 2.6 billion profit, the later stake sold entirely in November 2025 for 5.83 billion to fund OpenAI and Stargate. Draw the lessons about conviction, timing, and the difference between being early and being right.

chapters.title: Sovereign Money
chapters.brief: How state capital entered the industry at scale, what it wants, and what it changes. Cover subsidy programmes and sovereign investment vehicles descriptively. Avoid taking political sides; describe the mechanisms and the incentives.

chapters.title: What the Auditors See
chapters.brief: The chapter no other book on this subject will contain, and the author's home ground. Walk through the specific areas where auditors must exercise judgement in these companies, why each is difficult, and what a reader can infer from how a company discloses them. Written as general practice, naming no standard and no regulator, so it holds across jurisdictions.

chapters.title: The Map
chapters.brief: Draw the whole picture in one place: who owns stakes in whom, who supplies whom, and where the same company appears as supplier, customer and shareholder. State the date of the map explicitly and tell the reader plainly that it will be out of date, and how to redraw it themselves.

parts.title: Cycles, Risk and What Would Break It
parts.summary: The industry's own history is the best available guide to what happens next.

chapters.title: The Semiconductor Cycle

art.title: The cycle that has never stopped

chapters.brief: Explain the cycle properly, why it is structural rather than a failure of management, why capacity always arrives late, and why the industry has never escaped it despite believing several times that it had. This is the chapter that arms the reader against both euphoria and doom.

chapters.title: Four Previous Times People Were Certain
chapters.brief: Four episodes when this industry was certain demand was structural, and what happened. Tell each accurately and without smugness. The point is not that booms always end; it is that the arguments made now have been made before, and the reader should recognise them.

chapters.title: The Case That This Is a Bubble

art.title: The bear argument, stated at its strongest
labels: Capex far ahead of end revenue

chapters.brief: State the bear case as strongly and fairly as its most serious proponents make it. No strawmen. The book's credibility depends on this chapter being genuinely persuasive.

chapters.title: The Case That It Is Not

art.title: The bull argument, stated at its strongest
labels: Buyers are cash-generative, not leveraged startups
Adoption is early in the enterprise

chapters.brief: State the bull case with equal force and fairness. Then decline to adjudicate, and explain precisely which observable facts would move a careful reader toward one side or the other. Give the reader the test, not the verdict.

chapters.title: Concentration Risk

art.title: How much depends on how little
labels: One foundry at the leading edge

chapters.brief: Lay out the concentration honestly across every layer. This is not a prediction of failure; it is a description of how narrow the base of the pyramid is, and why that matters to anyone holding any part of it.

chapters.title: Taiwan
chapters.brief: Handle the most sensitive subject in the book with care and without speculation about politics or conflict. Describe what is manufactured there, why it cannot be moved quickly, what diversification has actually achieved, and how long a genuine alternative would take to build. Facts and timelines only.

chapters.title: Export Controls
chapters.brief: Describe the mechanisms and their observable effects on company strategy and supply chains, without advocating a position. Cover the second-order effects that are usually missed: acceleration of domestic substitution, and the incentive to design around a threshold rather than beneath it.

chapters.title: What Would Actually Break It

art.title: Failure modes worth watching
labels: Credit tightens for the financed buyers

chapters.brief: The chapter that replaces prediction with a watch list. Six specific, observable failure modes, what each would look like early, and where it would show up in the disclosures first. Practical, unsensational, and genuinely useful to someone holding any of these shares.

parts.title: The Future
parts.summary: What is durable in this analysis, and what a reader should watch after the numbers in this book have gone stale.

chapters.title: Where the Bottleneck Goes Next

art.title: The moving constraint
labels: The next one will be something else

chapters.brief: The single most useful framework for the future: the binding constraint moves, and the profit follows it. Trace where it has already moved, explain why it moves, and give the reader a way to spot the next one before the headlines do.

chapters.title: The Memory Decade

art.title: What a supercycle usually does next

chapters.brief: Return to memory with the reader now equipped. Assess seriously whether HBM's qualification requirements and technical difficulty genuinely break the historical cycle or merely lengthen it. Present both cases with the historical record in front of the reader, and note the capacity being committed now — including SK Hynix's reported 38 billion dollar investment — as the thing to watch.

chapters.title: Inference Economics

art.title: Why the cost per answer decides everything
labels: Cost per token falls with efficiency
Margin depends on which moves faster

chapters.brief: The economics that will determine whether the model layer becomes profitable. Explain the relationship between falling unit costs and expanding usage, why cheaper inference does not automatically mean lower revenue, and the conditions under which the model layer keeps margin rather than passing it all through.

chapters.title: Who Could Still Enter

art.title: Barriers by layer
labels: Semiconductor: capital and physics — very high

chapters.brief: Assess entry barriers layer by layer, and explain why the lowest barrier sits at the layer closest to the customer — which is exactly why margin there is hardest to defend. Cover realistic entrants and the conditions each would need.

chapters.title: What the Stack Might Look Like in 2030

art.title: Three scenarios, not a forecast
labels: In all three: someone owns the bottleneck

chapters.brief: Three coherent scenarios, each argued properly, with the indicators that would distinguish them. Explicitly not a prediction. Explain what all three have in common, and why that common element is the durable insight.

chapters.title: A Reader's Watch List

art.title: What to check, and how often
labels: Equipment orders as a leading signal

chapters.brief: The practical payoff of the whole book. Six things a reader can check themselves, where to find each, how often it updates, and what a change in it would mean. Turn the reader from a consumer of headlines into someone who can read the industry directly.

chapters.title: What the Numbers Cannot Tell You
chapters.brief: The closing chapter. Return to the book's founding discipline: every figure had a date, every claim had a source, and none of it removes the need for judgement. State plainly what this analysis can and cannot do, and end on the reader's own responsibility for any decision they take. No prediction, no exhortation, no sales pitch.
